claims.text: Short-range chemical ordering is present and operative in NbTaTiV-like refractory high-entropy alloys at elevated temperatures.
Short-range chemical ordering promotes edge-dislocation-mediated plasticity over screw-dislocation-mediated plasticity in NbTaTiV-like alloys.
Plastic deformation in single-BCC NbTaTiV at elevated temperatures is predominantly mediated by edge dislocations.
Edge dislocations account for the high strength and strength retention of NbTaTiV at elevated temperatures.
Short-range chemical ordering governs the high-temperature strength of NbTaTiV-like alloys.
Short-range chemical ordering governs the thermoelastic behavior of NbTaTiV-like alloys.
NbTaTiV exhibits temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation and measurable temperature-dependent elastic moduli.
Local chemical order modifies lattice friction encountered by dislocations.
Local chemical order raises the energy barriers for screw dislocations.
Raising screw-dislocation barriers favors edge-dislocation mobility and slip.
The target NbTaTiV alloy can remain a single-phase BCC solid solution under the relevant characterization conditions.
Conventional BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations.
A baseline BCC refractory alloy lacking significant short-range order will have weaker high-temperature strength retention because it lacks that ordering.
Relative to the proposed baseline, ordered NbTaTiV-like material will retain greater strength at elevated temperatures.
The ordered alloy will show sustained lattice-distortion signatures in in situ diffraction.
TEM observations of NbTaTiV-like material will reveal a predominance of edge dislocations over screw dislocations.
Diffraction, atom-probe tomography, and related analyses can detect or quantify short-range chemical order in concentrated alloys.
